title: JavaScript Basics
summary: Learn to write simple JavaScript programs using variables, operators, conditions, loops, arrays, objects and functions, and finish with a small class results project.
audience: Beginners aged 14 and up. No prior coding needed; a phone or tablet with a browser is enough

body.p: JavaScript is the language that makes web pages interactive, and it also runs phone apps and servers. You need nothing installed to learn it. Open any free online JavaScript editor or playground in your phone or computer browser, type the examples, run them, and compare what you see with the output shown here. Some editors show output in a panel called the console.
The command console.log prints a value so you can see it. Lines end with a semicolon in this course, which is a common habit.
A variable is a name that holds a value. Use const for a value that will not be given a new value, and let for one that will change. Here a school shop sells exercise books at 350 naira each.

Notice that quantity was changed with a plain = and no let the second time, because the variable already exists. Trying to give a new value to a const variable causes an error. This is useful: if you mark something const, JavaScript protects it from accidental changes. A good habit is to start with const and switch to let only when you know the value must change.

Variable names can use letters, digits, underscores and the dollar sign, cannot start with a digit, and are case sensitive, so Price and price are different. By convention, JavaScript programmers write names like examScore, with each new word starting with a capital letter.
Every value has a type. The typeof operator tells you which one JavaScript sees.

list: string: text inside quotes, such as "Accra" or 'Class 5B'.
number: every number, whole or decimal, is one type called number.
boolean: either true or false, written in lower case.
undefined: the value of a variable that was created but never given a value.

body.tip: One equals sign stores a value. Two or three equals signs compare values, which you will meet in the lesson on conditions.

body.p: Operators combine values. The arithmetic operators are + for add, - for subtract, * for multiply, / for divide, % for remainder and ** for power. The remainder operator is very useful: it gives what is left after dividing. For example, a taxi driver in Nairobi who has 17 passengers and cars that hold 5 can ask how many are left over.
Multiplication happens before addition, as in maths class, and brackets change the order. Short forms save typing: total += 50 means total = total + 50, and count++ adds one to count.

body.h: Joining text, and a famous surprise

body.p: The + operator also joins strings. When one side is text and the other is a number, JavaScript turns the number into text and joins them, rather than adding. This surprises many beginners. The minus operator only works on numbers, so it converts the text to a number instead.

The last line prints NaN, which stands for Not a Number. It is what you get when a conversion or calculation makes no sense. Use Number() to convert text, for example text typed by a user, before you calculate with it.
Computers store decimals in binary, so some sums are very slightly off. For money, round to the number of decimals you need with toFixed, which returns text such as 0.30.
Instead of joining many pieces with +, use backticks (the ` key) and put values inside ${ }. Anything inside the braces is calculated. This is called a template string.

body.tip: Quotes for template strings are backticks, not apostrophes. On many phone keyboards you find the backtick by long-pressing the apostrophe or on the symbols page.

lessons.title: Making decisions with if and else

body.p: Programs become useful when they choose what to do. An if statement runs a block of code only when a condition is true. A condition is anything that gives true or false, usually made with a comparison operator.

list: === means equal in value and type, and !== means not equal.
> and < mean greater than and less than; >= and <= include equal.
&& means and (both must be true), || means or (at least one), and ! means not.

body.p: Always use three equals signs, never two. The double version tries to convert types first and gives surprising answers, while the triple version compares exactly.
Here is a grading program like the ones teachers use. JavaScript checks the conditions from top to bottom and runs only the first block whose condition is true, then skips the rest.
Order matters. If the first test had been score >= 50, then a score of 85 would also get C, because it would match first. Put the strictest condition first.

JavaScript can treat any value as true or false in a condition. The values 0, an empty string, null, undefined and NaN count as false. Almost everything else counts as true. This lets you write short checks, for example whether a user typed a name.
The last example uses the conditional operator: condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse. It is a compact if and else for choosing one value.

body.tip: When a condition does not behave as expected, print the pieces with console.log to see what values you really have.

body.p: A loop repeats a block of code. Without loops you would need to write the same line a hundred times. JavaScript has several loops. The two you need first are for and while.
A for loop has three parts inside its brackets, separated by semicolons: where to start, when to keep going, and how to move on after each round. Here is a loop that adds up the numbers from 1 to 5.

Follow it by hand like a detective. Start: i is 1 and sum is 0. Round one adds 1, round two adds 2, and so on up to 5. When i becomes 6, the test i <= 5 is false and the loop stops. 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 is 15, which matches the output.
A market trader can use a loop to print a times table that helps price goods. Here is the 7 times table up to 3.
A while loop keeps going as long as its condition is true. Use it when you do not know in advance how many rounds are needed. Suppose you save 500 shillings a week and want at least 2000.

Be careful: if the condition can never become false, the loop runs forever and your browser tab may freeze. In the example, saved grows each round, so the condition eventually fails. If you forgot the line saved += 500, it would never stop. If this happens, close or reload the tab.
Inside a loop, break stops the loop immediately and continue skips to the next round.
Even numbers are skipped by continue. At 9, the break ends the loop, so only 1, 3, 5 and 7 are printed.

body.tip: Use let for the loop counter, not const, because the counter changes every round.

body.p: So far each variable held one value. Real programs hold collections. JavaScript has two main kinds: arrays for ordered lists, and objects for things with named properties.

An array is a list written in square brackets. Each item has a position called an index, and counting starts from 0, not 1. The length property tells you how many items there are, so the last item is at index length minus 1.

body.code:
mango
3
orange
4
mango, banana, orange, pawpaw

body.p: Even though fruits is declared with const, you can still add items with push. The const only stops you from replacing the whole array with something else. You can also loop over an array. The for...of loop gives you each item in turn.

Two methods are worth learning early. filter keeps only the items that pass a test, and map makes a new array by changing every item. Both take a small function written with an arrow, x => something, and neither changes the original array.
An object groups related facts under names, called keys. You read a value with a dot and the key. Objects can hold other objects and arrays.
A list of objects is how many apps store records, such as a class register: an array where each item is an object for one student.

body.code:
Zainab: pass
Peter: fail
Mwila: pass

body.tip: If you see undefined when reading an array or object, check the index or the spelling of the key. Keys are case sensitive.

lessons.title: Functions and a small final project

body.p: A function is a named, reusable recipe. You write it once and call it whenever you need it, with different inputs. The inputs are called parameters, and the result sent back is the return value.
The word return sends a value out and ends the function. A very common bug is forgetting return. The function then gives back undefined, even though the calculation was done.

A variable created with let or const inside curly braces exists only inside them. This is called scope. It keeps functions tidy, because their private variables cannot clash with others. Functions can also be written in a shorter arrow form, which you already met in filter and map.

body.h: Final project idea: a class results calculator

body.p: Combine everything from this course in one small program. A teacher has a list of students with marks. Your program should print each student with a grade, the class average, and the best student. Build it in small steps, running after each one.

steps: Create an array of objects, each with a name and a score.
Write a function grade(score) using if, else if and else, like the one in the conditions lesson.
Loop through the array with for...of and print a template string with the name, score and grade.
Add up all scores in a loop and divide by the array length to get the average.
Track the highest score in a variable and the name that goes with it, updating inside the loop.
Wrap the whole thing in a function so you can try it with different classes.

body.p: Here is a short version of the core, so you can check your own work.

body.code:
Amina 78 A
Tunde 54 C
Grace 41 Fail
Average: 57.7
Best: Amina

body.tip: When you finish, extend it: add a pass mark variable with const, count how many students failed, or change the marks and check your results by hand.

options: Nothing; it works and a is 6

quiz.q:
What does this code print?
console.log("5" + 3);

What does this code print?
console.log("5" - 3);

What does this code print?
console.log(0 == "0", 0 === "0");

options: It causes a syntax error because while needs a semicolon
It never stops, because saved never changes
It causes an error because a is const

quiz.q: A bus holds 5 people. What does console.log(17 % 5) print for 17 people, and what does it mean?
options: 2 - the people left over after filling 3 buses
12 - the remaining people after one bus
